Our expectations were proven right, although the correction came both later and was more limited than we had expected. Prices briefly dipped below $6,000/tonne in late September/early October, before strong support emerged at that level. Since then, spot copper has trended upwards, peaking just short of $7,000/tonne on 23rd November, 151% up on its trough in late December last year. LME Stocks & Copper Price

Investors continue to provide essential fuel to the sustained strength of copper prices. Buying from this source has been driven by expectations of a tight copper market going forward as well as the weakness of the dollar. The market’s immediate fundamentals on the other hand have failed to show any material improvement since our previous Quarterly, as the much-discussed consumption recovery has yet to up its pace, outside of China. Indicative of the questionable supply-demand conditions that characterise the market, we note that around 188,000 tonnes of refined copper have been added to stocks held at exchange-approved warehouses, including LME, Comex and Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) from end-August and through to the time of writing, 30th November. This brings the overall increase in exchange stocks this year-to-date to over 232,000 tonnes. The above-mentioned increases were in small part offset by a modest decline in other reported stocks. There has however been a build of unreported inventories in China, in addition to the 235,000 tonnes purchased by the Chinese State Reserve Bureau (SRB), which GFMS treat as consumption in our statistics. All this largely confirms the 366 tonne surplus GFMS estimate for the first three quarters of the year as well as our projections for oversupply of 28 tonnes in the final quarter. This compares with the International Copper Study Group’s (ICSG) estimates of a 186,000 tonne deficit over the first seven months of the year, which suffers from distortions related to the stocking cycle in China. Considering the outlook for copper’s fundamentals, although it is hard to argue a bearish long term outlook, given the structural constraints to mine production in place, the same cannot be said for the shorter-term. Star

ting with production, the current developments on the industrial action front, which has over the last couple of months been a key issue for the market, are if anything suggestive of some of the constraints being eased. We note that BHP Billiton recently reached a wage deal with workers at its Spence mine in Chile, the last of a number of such deadlocks copper mining had been facing since late summer. Moving to demand and starting with China, that has spearheaded any recovery copper consumption has enjoyed this year-to-date, there are growing signs that the aforementioned inventory build is finally beginning to filter through to apparent consumption. Copper imports have been broadly trending downwards since they peaked in June and we expect this to continue in the last two months of the year. Elsewhere, consumption growth outside China has yet to really take off and this seems unlikely to materialise until well into 2010. **3** Independent - Informed - International 3-Year Copper Forecast - November 2009 **CONFIDENTIAL** LME Stocks as Weeks of Consumption

The heavy reliance on the investor sector highlights the downside risks for copper prices in the short term. Indeed, our price projections for the final quarter are conditional on such a correction taking place before the end of the year. Relating to the metal’s solid longer term fundamentals, we would expect such corrections to trigger strong buying by investors (and to some extent also consumers), providing the floor for copper prices, from which mini-rallies can develop. A volatile but generally trending upwards trajectory for copper prices will most likely remain in place throughout 2010 and, to some extent, through to the end of the forecast period. ###### **1.2 Market Background** Copper prices were among the last of the base metals to peak at $8,985/tonne on July 3 2008. Since then, the performance of the price of the metal has been remarkably similar to the rest of the sector. Over the six months following the peak, copper prices gave up the bulk of their gains, falling to a low of $2,770/tonne in December. Since then, they have recovered the bulk of their losses, leading the recovery of the wider base metals sector and recently peaking at around $7,000/ tonne. Before discussing our projections on copper supply and demand as well as our expectations on prices, it is worth providing a brief overview of the conditions that have affected the market recently and that we feel remain relevant going forward: 1. The main theme in the copper market has been the battle between tight supply and the weak demand environment. 2. The former largely relates to grade problems and industrial action affecting Chilean output a

nd African Copper-belt production failing to live up to potential. 3. Despite all relevant economic indicators pointing to a recovery and consumption has indeed come off its lows, it remains far below ‘normal’ levels in most key markets for copper, with the notable exception of China. A key condition that differentiates copper from other base metals is that for much of the first half of the year, its LME inventories were on a declining trend. This changed in the summer and stocks have been rising from mid-July and through to the present time. 5. The decline in LME inventories and their subsequent increase were respectively caused by Chinese imports rising to unprecedented levels and more recently falling (although they remain historically high to-date). As is discussed in detail in Chapter 2, the OECD Composite Leading Indicators, manufacturing PMI and other forward-looking indicators relating to industrial production have and continue to suggest demand conditions in mature economies are set to improve. Elsewhere, the data for China suggests that the recovery that has been underway for some time is still going strong, although apparent demand may be affected in the short term by the inventory adjustment process. 6. In addition to changes in reported inventories, anecdotal evidence suggests that a substantial stockpile of copper has been accumulated in China this year-todate. Given the on-going uncertainty in the economic and financial markets (the problems in Dubai being the most recent illustration of these), we highlight three different scenarios: 7. Despite the above, reported stocks stand at less than three weeks’ global consumption and in our view the above-mentioned Chinese unreported inventories are significantly lower. 8. Strong investor interest has underpinned prices over the better part of this year. Investors have been increasingly forward looking. ###### **1.3 Economic Assumptions** GFMS’ view on how the global macroeconomic backdrop will develop over the forecast period holds paramount importance for our projections for copper supply, demand and prices. At the time of writing, the majority of relevant economic indicators continue to paint a largely positive picture for copper demand, e

ven though to-date a noteworthy recovery has yet to commence in the most key markets outside China. **Base case:** (with a 45% probability outcome). We have revised the projections of our Base Case upwards somewhat since the previous edition of our 3-Year Copper Forecast, in response to the better than expected results over the last few months. Due to the severity of the recession in the first half of the year, global GDP is expected to fall by 1.6% overall in real terms this year. The recovery that has already commenced is still expected to gather momentum in 2010, helped by re-stocking, and we expect global GDP to increase by 2% in real terms over the year. Further acceleration is forecast for 2011, but in the last year of the forecast period, as the impact of the stimulus packages wanes, a slow-down is expected. LME Stocks vs Monthly Average Price

A more robust recovery followed by stronger growth is the principal assumption of our most bullish scenario. As real GDP growth in most mature economies breaches the 2% mark in 2010 and China tops 9%, global GDP growth is seen rising by 3.3% over the year, accelerating to nearly 4% in 2011 and keeping to a healthy 3.5% in the last year of the period. The higher growth is expected to come at the expense of strong inflation, particularly in the US, where consumer price inflation peaks at 8.5% in 2011. **Scenario C:** (with a 25% probability outcome). Under our most pessimistic (and in our view least likely) scenario, the current buoyancy in the markets proves unjustified, and the recovery proves anaemic, particularly when the private sector takes on the reins. Global GDP declines by more than 2% this year, before recovering by an uninspiring 1.0% and 1.6% in 2010 and 2011. Even in the final year of the forecast period, growth, at 2.3%, falls short of the 2000-2008 average of around 4%. It is worth noting that under this scenario, inflation keeps to extremely low levels throughout 2010-2012, after being in negative territory this year overall. ###### **1.4 The Dollar** The dollar has continued to weaken against the euro since our last publication, with the rate recently topping 1.50, at which level it met strong resistance. The issues noted in our previous quarterly, namely concern

s over a period of strong inflation, in the aftermath of a policy of quantitative easing in the US, as well as a heightened risk appetite impacting the safe haven appeal of the US dollar have continued to weigh on the greenback. Elsewhere, the emergence of the US currency as the new carry trade currency has also contributed to the trend. In GFMS’ view, the recent peak in the dollar:euro rate overshot its mark and a correction cannot be rulled out. The very recent crisis in Dubai illustrates the fragile nature of the global economic recovery and the potential for bouts of risk aversion, albeit short lived, to emerge. Nevertheless, we continue to see the dollar remain by and large weak from now and through to well into the second half of 2010, resulting in a low-field 1.42 average for next year. Eventually, as the global economy starts to return to more normal conditions we expect the dollar to strengthen from its low starting point. As inflation begins to accelerate in 2011, we would expect the US monetary authorities to react with higher interest rates, which would likely push the country’s currency into a cyclical recovery. In 2012, we expect the dollar:euro rate to average 1.26. Under Scenario B, the dollar is forecast to weaken further, largely as a result of exceptionally low levels of risk aversion. Under this scenario, the recent emergence of the dollar carry trend is continued and indeed extended. Thus the dollar weakens even further than under the base case this year, to average $1.39/€ before averages of $1.50 and $1.65 in 2010 and 2011 respectively. In contrast, the swift return of risk aversion under Scenario C sees the dollar beginning to appreciate as early as next year. Global Consumption vs Spot Price

This trend is certainly still in place. In late November, prices are higher than in August even though LME inventories are 46% higher than their endAugust levels, As GFMS have often noted, the opaque nature of metals investments makes it is hard to quantify its impact on prices. In the case of base metals, where the o

verwhelming bulk of activity is essentially unreported, the task becomes ever more difficult. Nevertheless, using what limited data is available and combining that with anecdotal information, that we obtain through field research, conjectures on the direction and relevance of investor activity in copper can be made. As noted earlier in this introduction, investor attitudes towards copper have been very positive this year-todate and this has been instrumental in maintaining the price’s upward trajectory. In addition, it is our understanding that investor buying has also affected forward prices, as investors have been increasingly buying further along the curve and in doing so have boosted the contango. Although among the LME metals, copper is certainly the most favoured metal by investors, the bulk of investment activity on the metal comprises part of a strategy on the wider sector and in most cases indeed commodities in general sector. Such strategies can be passive, meaning that a specific basket of commodities that contains a certain weighting of copper, or active, meaning that allocations across commodities are constantly varied according to the managers’ views and often contain both long and short positions. As a result of the above, copper prices often show relatively strong correlations with other commodity prices. This is illustrated in the graph below, that features rolling 20-day correlation coefficients between copper prices and the Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI) as well as the Dow-Jones UBS Commodity Index (DJ-UBSCI). The horizontal lines in the chart are the boundaries outside which the correlation coefficients are statistically significant. According to the graph, the link seems to have been strong over much of the second half of this year, although it recently collapsed and even turned negative, as copper-specific issues underpinned prices, despite the wider commodities sector having, at least for the time being, run out of steam. Indicative of the growth of copper investment is the uptrend recorded in net long positions held by investors in copper futures listed on the Comex. Although activity on the exchange accounts for only a small portion of the global copper investment market, the data still provides a useful proxy to overall activity. Data on weekly net positions is provided in the chart below. Within commodities investments, index investments have been a particularly successful vehicle for funds and other entities gaining exposure on the sector. The lion’s share within this universe is undoubtedly taken by the two indices mentioned above, GSCI and DJ-UBSCI. Both these indices contain weightings in copper, the former amounting to 3.56% and the latter to 7.31%. Although part of the $52 billion increase noted between the end of last year and the third quarter of 2009 was related to rising prices, GFMS are certain that a significant portion reflects inflows of new funds. It is worth also noting that anecdotal evidence suggests that this has continued through to the present time. Considering the issues that currently drive investor interest in copper, expectations of a noteworthy improvement in the metal’s fundamentals continue to be the single most important feature. This is in part related to the positive outlook of the demandside fundamentals of the wider base metals sector, underpinned by expectations that strong growth will continue in China. In the case of copper, this is augmented by expectations of production growth proving limited, in line with past experience. Apart from the supportive underlying fundamentals, the weakness of the greenback as well as concerns over inflation have both been issues that have led investors to “hard” assets and this has certainly benefited copper. Going forward, GFMS expect investors to continue to have a positive impact on the copper market for the foreseeable future. Although at the time of writing there are signs that the market may be overheated, suggesting a correction may well be on the cards, as we noted earlier fresh buying will most probably appear at the dip, providing a solid floor for prices, which we would be surprised to see fall below $6,000/tonne. As conditions improve into 2010, the overall appetite for copper investments will most probably grow. Although liquidations will continue to take place throughout, as the “smart” money takes profits, the majority of such moves will probably be part of a twoway trading strategies, with an overall bias towards the long side. Looking further ahead, we believe that over the last two years of the forecast period, investors will most probably remain interested in commodities. Moreover, the exceptionally bullish fundamentals of copper will likely continue to make it a favourite. As such, our projections for copper prices in 2011 and 2012 see a considerable degree of volatility and levels arguably higher than the s

uply-demand deficits alone could justify. 

A key wildcard that could materially affect copper investment demand over the course of the forecast period will be the approval and potential success of the physically backed listed fund, not dissimilar to the precious metals ETFs but closed-ended, that ScotiaMocatta filed for last summer.  Rather than satisfying any desire by investors to hold physical metal instead of futures or other derivatives, such a product would allow certain types of investors who are not allowed to invest in futures and options, such as the majority of pension funds, to access the copper market for the first time. 

It is of course arguable that the size of the copper market is too small for such investors to enter it, but one can certainly not rule out a marginal allocation by some may be made.  Although marginal in relation to their overall holdings, such allocations could have a noteworthy impact on copper prices.  In addition, as such holdings would be relatively inert, they would likely comprise a long term “core” long position and by implication have a longer lasting effect on copper prices.  We note that as it is still very early to assess the likelihood that the above will take place, GFMS have not included the launch and success of a physically backed copper product.

###### **1.6 Consumption** 

We have revised our estimates and projections for global copper consumption in 2009 downwards somewhat since the previous release of our quarterly forecast, as a pick up in demand in the mature economies has been slow to emerge.  We now expect demand to total 17.673 million tonnes this year, down 2% year-on-year. 

After a notable rise in the second quarter, our figures see the quarter-on-quarter growth remain contained through to the second half of next year, when the recovery in countries outside China is expected to really kick in, compounding ongoing growth in the former. Overall, demand in 2010 is forecast to exceed 19 million tonnes, posting an 8.4% year-on-year increase and registering a new all-time high. 

More contained, although still above-trend, growth is forecast in both the final two years of the forecast period, amounting to 4.9% and 3.9% respectively. By 2012, GFMS expect global consumption to have reached 20.886 million tonnes, 15% higher than the previous record high of 2007 

###### **1.7 Production** 

Although we are aware of the plethora of planned expansions to mining capacity over the course of the forecast period, GFMS have once again opted to err on the side of caution with regards to the results these efforts will yield, clearly influenced by the history of the sector.  For this year, as a result of lower grades, technical difficulties, industrial action and to some extend the price-related cutbacks seen early in the year, all of which were compounded by a tighter scrap market, w

e see production register a modest decline of 2% to reach 18.067 million tonnes. As many of the above-mentioned exogenous constraints are overcome and boosted by genuine growth in mine capacity, production is forecast to register its biggest increase since the start of the millennium, of 5.7% to 19.089 million tonnes next year. Healthy increases are also noted in the final two years of the forecast period, when production is seen growing by 4.6% and 3.9% respectively, leaving output at 20.744 million tonnes in 2012. The bulk of the growth is due to mine capacity expansions in the African copperbelt. Significant contributions are also provided by Chile and Peru. |

###### **1.8 Market Outlook** ###### **Base Case Scenario** Despite having revised our Chinese consumption projections upwards, this has been more than offset by the downwards revisions to our mature economies demand, due to the evidence suggesting a material recovery has yet to commence in these markets. Although we have also amended our production estimates/projections, to show a lower global total for the year, the extent of this revision has been smaller, and this has resulted in our 2009 surplus having increased from 245,000 tonnes in our previous quarterly forecast to 393,000 tonnes. In addition to the above

, the higher surplus figure is now closer to our estimates of the growth in combined reported and Chinese unreported stocks this year (excluding SRB stocks which we treat as consumption, due to our understanding that they are relatively inert). Specifically, to-date reported stocks have grown by a little over 200,000 tonnes and we would be surprised if further inflows did not take place later in the year. In addition to that, we are convinced that a significant unreported stock build-up took place in China earlier in the year. Although these inventories are most likely declining at the moment, on a net basis the year will almost certainly see a net increase. On a quarterly basis, our estimates suggest that almost all the oversupply this year occurred in the first half. Again, this is largely confirmed by changes in reported stocks as well as our own estimates of flows into and out of Chinese unreported inventories. Indeed, the second half of the year has seen a market very close to balance, although the recent recovery in mine production, as some of the industrial action issues have been resolved, brought an end to this in the final quarter. Ongoing increases in mine production are the key driver for the surpluses seen in the first two quarter of next year. Later in 2010, as the recovery in mature economies’ consumption is added to continued steady increases in the developing world, demand catches up, resulting in a virtually balanced third quarter. As supply in the final quarter of the year fails to grow as fast as consumption, the market records its first deficit since the second quarter of 2008, with demand exceeding supply by 158,000 tonnes. ###### **2.6  Scenario C** 

Scenario C sees a protracted and sluggish improvement in growth in almost all economies, as the after effects of the credit crunch linger.  Fundamentally, the global economy is caught in a disinflationary trap, where the effect of the measures taken by central banks and governments do not feed through into growth in the economy.  In the latter part of the forecast, it also assumes that the fiscal pressures ensure that this element of support for the economy cannot be maintained at prior levels. 

Under this outcome, the global economy contracts by 2.0% this year and only grows by a very modest 1.0% in 2010.  In the last two years of the forecast, the growth rate does quicken to 1.6% and then to 2.3% but this is still below the growth rate in any year between 2002 and 2008.  It is worth noting that, unlike the other scenarios, growth accelerates in 2012, as central banks do not need to take stringent measures to slow overheating economies. 

The troubled **US economy** is central to this view, in particular the heavily indebted consumer and federal government.  As exemplified by the latest US retail sales data, the legacy of the excessive spending and incredibly low levels of personal saving over many years is constraining the US consumer.  This could continue throughout, not least as unemployment is already at its highest level since the early 1980s and is set to continue to rise until at least the second half of 2010.  Consequently, US GDP growth is forecast to be a minuscule 0.2% next year, followed by a hardly impressive 1.0% and 1.3% in 2011 and 2012 respectively. 

Similarly, **Japan** ’s economy is also hamstrung by weak exports under this scenario, as well as the continued difficulties of deflation in this country.  Given the bleak outlook, we forecast its GDP to only grow by a combined 1.75% over the next three years, after a sharp 6.5% drop this year.
